screens.title: Memory Management & Asset Optimization
screens.subtitle: Make your game fit the device: reduce memory, avoid GC spikes, and load content selectively.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on one of the most practical sources of performance problems: memory. You will learn how Unity counts memory for textures, audio, meshes, animations and runtime objects, and how to make trade-offs that keep your game stable across devices. We will examine texture resolution and platform compression choices, when to use mip maps, how to pick audio load types and compression, and how to reduce runtime allocations so garbage collection does not cause hitches. You will also learn how to use Asset Bundles to load and unload content at runtime, which is essential for large or downloadable games. Throughout, we use concrete examples: reducing a 4096 texture to a 1024 max size, switching a long music track from full decompression to streaming, and checking the Memory profiler to confirm each change. By the end you will know what to measure, how to change import settings, and how to validate improvements on target hardware. Think about a mobile device with limited R A M: which asset decisions will prevent crashes or long load times?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Most memory problems come from assets. Optimize textures, audio, meshes, and manage runtime allocations to avoid GC spikes and crashes.

Second, you will learn to choose texture compression and maximum sizes for different platforms, balancing visual quality and memory. Third, you will apply audio import settings like streaming or compressed-in-memory to keep long music tracks from exhausting R A M. Fourth, you will perform mesh and animation compression steps in the Model Import Settings to shrink asset size. screens.title: Why memory matters in Unity
screens.subtitle: Definition, symptoms, and a simple diagnostic checklist

narration.text: Memory determines whether your game runs smoothly on a device. In Unity, memory is consumed by assets such as textures, audio, meshes and animation data, by scene and runtime data, and by allocations your code creates. When memory usage is too high you may see long load times, stuttering during gameplay, or outright crashes on low-R A M devices. A basic diagnostic checklist is: open the Memory profiler, take a snapshot, note which category — Textures, Audio, Meshes, or Scripting — is largest, and test on the target device rather than only in the editor. For example, a mobile device with 2 GB of R A M can behave very differently than the editor on your desktop. A common misconception is that only file size on disk matters; in Unity, runtime memory is about how assets are represented in R A M after import, decoded formats, and mipmap allocation. Remember that uncompressed textures and decompressed audio can balloon in memory even if their compressed disk sizes were small. Takeaway: always measure first, change import settings second, and verify the memory reduction with the profiler on device. What would you measure first on a device that stutters at level load?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Memory problems manifest as load delays, frame hitches, and crashes; measure with the Memory profiler to find the largest consumers.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why memory matters in Unity
Symptoms, causes, and an actionable checklist for measurement.
Quick checklist
  • Open Memory profiler and take a snapshot.
  • Identify largest categories: Textures, Audio, Meshes, Scripting.
  • Test on the target device, not only in editor.
Common misconception
Compressed file size does not equal runtime memory. Uncompressed representations and mip maps determine RAM cost.
Example
A 4096 texture may look fine on desktop but can push a mobile device over its memory limit. Reducing Max Size to 1024 or 512 often yields big savings with little perceptible quality loss for distant or small objects.
Key Takeaway

Measure first. Optimize the biggest categories first, and re-measure on device to confirm improvements.

Annotated memory map
Textures
Often the largest category; check Max Size, format, and mip maps.
Audio
Long music should stream; effects can decompress on load.
Meshes & Animations
Reduce vertex count, enable mesh optimization, and apply animation compression.
Why test on device?
Editor memory uses host machine resources; a profiler snapshot on target hardware reveals the true peak memory constraints.

screens.title: Texture resolution and compression
screens.subtitle: How Max Size and compression formats impact memory and quality

narration.text: Textures are usually the largest single memory consumers in a Unity project. The two levers you control are resolution and compression format. Resolution affects pixel count directly: dropping a texture from 4096 to 1024 reduces its pixel area by sixteen times, which usually reduces memory dramatically with small visual cost when the texture is used on distant or small objects. Compression formats are platform-specific: Desktop often uses DXT which balances quality and size; Android commonly uses ETC or ETC2; iOS uses PVRTC. Uncompressed RGBA 32-bit uses the most memory and should be reserved for UI elements or cases where compression artifacts are unacceptable. Another important option is mip maps: they add approximately 33% memory overhead but improve G P U sampling and reduce aliasing for textures viewed at various distances. A common mistake is enabling 4K uncompressed textures by default. A concrete example: take a 4096 albedo map for a far background object — reducing Max Size to 1024 and using ETC2 or PVRTC will usually produce a negligible visual difference while dramatically reducing texture memory. Closing question: which textures in your scene are visible at full screen size and therefore deserve higher resolution?

keyIdea.title: Texture rule of thumb
keyIdea.text: Reduce resolution to match on-screen size and use platform-native compression formats; reserve uncompressed textures for critical UI or high-fidelity needs.

content.html:
Comparison
Resolution vs Compression
Choose an appropriate Max Size and format per platform to balance memory and quality.
Resolution
Lower Max Size when the texture is not viewed full-screen. 512 or 256 may be enough for small or distant items.
Compression formats
Choose DXT for desktop, ETC/ETC2 for Android, PVRTC for iOS. These use GPU-friendly formats and reduce memory footprint.
Mip maps
Enable for textures seen at variable distances. Cost ~33% more memory but improves sampling and reduces aliasing.
Example
A background rock texture set to 4096 can be reduced to 1024 or 512 with ETC2 on Android to save memory while keeping acceptable visual fidelity.
Common mistake
Using uncompressed 32-bit textures for everything because they look best in the editor. This causes large runtime memory use on devices.
Platform format quick guide
Desktop - DXT
Good balance of quality and size for PC builds.
Android - ETC/ETC2
Use ETC/ETC2 to match mobile GPU expectations and save memory.
iOS - PVRTC
PVRTC is optimized for iOS devices but has different artifact characteristics; test visually.
Key Takeaway

Match texture resolution to on-screen size and use the GPU-native compression format for your target platform.

screens.title: Mip maps: trade-offs and best practices
screens.subtitle: When mip maps save GPU work and when to disable them

narration.text: Mip maps are pre-calculated, smaller versions of a texture used automatically when an object appears smaller on-screen. They improve visual quality by preventing aliasing and they can improve G P U performance because the G P U samples a smaller texture when appropriate. The trade-off is memory: enabling mip maps typically increases texture memory by about a third. Best practice is to enable mip maps for textures that will be viewed at multiple distances — terrain, characters, and distant objects that might move closer — and disable them for UI elements or textures that are always drawn at a 1:1 pixel ratio. A concrete example: a terrain diffuse map should usually have mip maps so the G P U uses lower-resolution levels when the camera is far away, while a HUD icon should not generate mip maps because the icon is always sharp at fixed screen pixels. A common mistake is enabling mip maps for every texture without considering UI and sprite atlases, which wastes memory. Final takeaway: enable mip maps when distance sampling improves quality or performance, and remember to account for the roughly 33% additional memory cost when planning your budgets.

keyIdea.title: Mip map rule
keyIdea.text: Enable for variable-distance textures; disable for UI or always-screen-size textures to avoid unnecessary memory overhead.

content.html:
Definition
Mip maps: trade-offs and best practices
Understand when lower-resolution levels help and when they harm your memory budget.
How mip maps work
They are precomputed downsampled versions of a texture that the GPU selects based on screen size to avoid aliasing and improve sampling speed.
Example
A character texture with mip maps uses smaller levels when the character is distant, reducing GPU texture sampling cost and improving visual smoothness at range.
When to disable
UI sprites, icons, and textures displayed at exact pixel sizes should not use mip maps because they increase memory without benefit.
Key Takeaway

Enable mip maps for variable-distance textures and accept the ~33% memory increase as a trade-off for better sampling and performance.

Quick decision guide
Enable mip maps
Terrain, characters, world textures that are seen at many distances.
Disable mip maps
HUD graphics, icons, and textures rendered at fixed screen pixels.
Memory impact
Expect roughly a 33% increase in memory for textures when mip maps are generated.

screens.title: Optimizing audio assets
screens.subtitle: Compression, load types, and sample rate choices

narration.text: Audio can also consume a lot of memory if you leave long tracks decompressed. The Audio Import Settings expose three primary controls: compression format, load type, and sample rate. For compression format, Vorbis is usually a good size/quality balance for music and long clips; ADPCM gives smaller sizes at reduced quality and can be effective for short sound effects. Load type has three behaviors: decompress on load, compressed in memory, and streaming. Decompress on load places the full uncompressed clip into R A M and is appropriate only for short effects. Compressed in memory keeps audio compressed in R A M and decompresses briefly during playback. Streaming reads chunks from disk during playback and is ideal for long background music or dialogues because it keeps R A M usage low. Additionally, lowering the sample rate for ambient or distant sounds from 44.1 kHz to 22 kHz can reduce memory and disk size with acceptable quality loss. A concrete lab action: import a 5-minute WAV, switch Load Type to Streaming, choose Vorbis with quality around 70 to 80 percent, then compare Memory profiler snapshots before and after to confirm reduced audio memory. A common misconception is that streaming always hurts C P U — it has some overhead, but the memory benefits for long tracks are usually worth it.

keyIdea.title: Audio optimization
keyIdea.text: Use streaming for long music, Vorbis for a good quality/size balance, and reduce sample rate where high fidelity is unnecessary.

content.html:
Process Flow
Optimizing audio assets
Follow these steps to minimize audio memory while keeping acceptable quality.
  1. Inspect the audio clip and note its length and current memory cost in the profiler snapshot.
  2. Compression — choose Vorbis for music or ADPCM for small sfx where size matters more than fidelity.
  3. Load Type — set Streaming for long tracks, Decompress On Load for short sfx, Compressed In Memory for medium clips.
  4. Sample Rate — lower to 22 kHz for distant/ambient sounds to save memory with modest quality loss.
  5. Re-measure in the Memory profiler on device and compare before/after snapshots.
Example
A 5-minute WAV set to Decompress On Load consumes large RAM. Switching to Streaming and Vorbis reduces peak memory dramatically.
Common mistake
Leaving long music as decompressed audio increases load times and memory; streaming is usually the safer choice for long clips.
Audio import quick cards
Decompress On Load
Best for short sound effects; places full uncompressed data in RAM.
Compressed In Memory
Keeps compressed data in RAM and decodes during playback; good for medium clips.
Streaming
Reads audio from disk in small chunks, ideal for long music and dialogue to minimize RAM.

screens.title: Mesh and animation data optimization
screens.subtitle: Vertex counts, mesh optimization, blend shapes, and animation compression

narration.text: Meshes and animations can quietly add up to significant memory cost. Mesh memory depends on vertex count, vertex attributes, and index buffers. Use Level of Detail (LOD) models so distant objects use much simpler meshes, remove unused blend shapes, and enable mesh optimization in the Model Import Settings to reorder vertices for better G P U cache behavior. For animations, Unity's import options allow different compression schemes such as keyframe reduction or Optimal compression; these reduce animation track sizes by removing redundant keyframes or encoding curves more compactly. A concrete scenario: a high-poly character with many blend shapes may consume large memory; remove unused blend shapes and enable animation keyframe reduction to shrink both disk and runtime memory. A common misconception is that reducing mesh detail always breaks visual quality; if you use LODs and smoothly swap models based on distance, the player rarely notices the lower-detail meshes at range. Takeaway: optimize meshes and animations through import-time options and LODs so you reduce memory without hurting perceived fidelity. Mesh and animation data optimization means use lods, remove unused blend shapes, and apply animation compression to cut asset memory while preserving visible quality.. In practical terms, vertex counts, mesh optimization, blend shapes, and animation compression. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mesh & animation rule
keyIdea.text: Use LODs, remove unused blend shapes, and apply animation compression to cut asset memory while preserving visible quality.

content.html:
Definition
Mesh and animation data optimization
Reduce vertex data and animation keyframes to lower memory usage.
Mesh tips
Use LODs to swap to simpler meshes at distance and enable Optimize Mesh in import settings to improve GPU cache locality.
Animation compression
Choose Optimal or Keyframe Reduction to remove redundant data and shrink animation memory cost.
Example
Removing unused blend shapes from a character and applying animation keyframe reduction noticeably lowers memory while keeping motion fidelity.
Key Takeaway

Optimize mesh complexity and animation data at import time, and use LODs to hide complexity when appropriate.

Checklist
Enable Optimize Mesh
Reorder vertices for GPU efficiency in Model Import Settings.
Remove unused blend shapes
Eliminate morph targets you don't animate to save memory.
Apply animation compression
Choose keyframe reduction or Optimal to shrink animation size.

screens.title: Using the Unity Memory Profiler
screens.subtitle: Capture, interpret, and act on memory snapshots

narration.text: The Memory Profiler is the tool you use to see which assets and systems use memory in your game. Start by capturing a snapshot in Window → Analysis → Profiler → Memory while running on your target device. In the snapshot, inspect the major categories: Textures, Meshes, Audio, Materials, and Scripting. Pay special attention to Total Allocated versus Used memory to understand headroom and fragmentation. When you see frequent garbage collection spikes, open the Scripting allocations list and look for allocations per frame. A recommended workflow: capture a baseline snapshot, change a single import setting such as texture Max Size or audio Load Type, run the same scenario, and capture a second snapshot. Compare the two snapshots to quantify memory savings. For example, switching a long music clip to streaming should show a significant drop in the Audio category. A common error is relying on editor-only snapshots; always test on the device because memory layout and G P U formats differ. Takeaway: use careful, repeatable profiler snapshots before and after changes so your optimizations are measurable and repeatable. Using the Unity Memory Profiler means capture snapshots on target hardware, compare before/after, and prioritize optimizations based on largest categories and scripting allocations.. In practical terms, capture, interpret, and act on memory snapshots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Profiler workflow
keyIdea.text: Capture snapshots on target hardware, compare before/after, and prioritize optimizations based on largest categories and scripting allocations.

content.html:
Process Flow
Using the Unity Memory Profiler
A repeatable measurement workflow to validate memory optimizations.
  1. Run the app on the target device and open the Memory profiler.
  2. Capture a baseline snapshot during a representative scenario.
  3. Change one import setting or optimization at a time.
  4. Capture a second snapshot and compare categories like Textures and Audio.
  5. Repeat until the largest consumers are within your budget.
Example
After reducing texture Max Size from 4096 to 1024, compare snapshots to see the Textures category drop and free memory for other systems.
Misconception
A single snapshot is not enough; compare before and after to prove impact and avoid chasing invisible changes.
Snapshot tips
Capture representative states
Take snapshots during loading, mid-play, and after level setup to see peak usage.
Compare categories
Look at Textures, Audio, Meshes, and Scripting allocations to prioritize work.
Watch for GC spikes
Frequent garbage collection indicates runtime allocation churn you should eliminate.

screens.title: Avoiding runtime allocations and GC hitches
screens.subtitle: Object pooling, reuse, and allocation hygiene

narration.text: Frequent allocations during gameplay cause the garbage collector to run often, producing frame-time spikes. Examples of problematic allocations include creating lists, strings, or temporary GameObjects inside Update loops. The solution is allocation hygiene: reuse collections instead of newing them, avoid generating temporary strings every frame, and use object pools for frequently spawned objects. Object pooling means creating a cache of reusable objects at startup and reactivating them when needed instead of instantiating and destroying repeatedly. For example, a shooter spawning many bullets per second should pull bullet instances from a pool and return them when the bullet is no longer active. A common misconception is that modern garbage collectors are cheap enough to ignore; in games with tight frame budgets, GC pauses are very noticeable. Verification: add instrumentation to count allocations per frame or inspect the Profiler's scripting allocations to confirm that pooling reduced per-frame allocations and eliminated GC spikes. Takeaway: lower runtime allocations through reuse and pooling to avoid unpredictable frame hitches during gameplay. Avoiding runtime allocations and GC hitches means reduce per-frame allocations by reusing objects, pooling frequently created instances, and avoiding temporary allocations in tight loops.. In practical terms, object pooling, reuse, and allocation hygiene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Allocation hygiene
keyIdea.text: Reduce per-frame allocations by reusing objects, pooling frequently created instances, and avoiding temporary allocations in tight loops.

content.html:
Process Flow
Avoiding runtime allocations and GC hitches
Practical patterns to stop frequent garbage collection pauses.
Problem
Allocating new objects inside Update() or other hot paths creates garbage that triggers the collector and causes frame-time spikes.
Solutions
  • Reuse List and array instances instead of newing them each frame.
  • Use object pools for bullets, effects, and frequently spawned items.
  • Avoid generating temporary strings or LINQ allocations in hot paths.
Example
A pooled bullet system reuses existing objects, reducing Instantiate/Destroy calls and eliminating per-frame allocations from creation and teardown.
Key Takeaway

Eliminate frequent allocations in hot paths. Use pooling and reuse to avoid GC spikes that interrupt gameplay.

Quick anti-patterns
Avoid in Update()
Creating new Lists, strings, or calling ToArray creates allocations every frame.
Prefer pooling
Pre-create reusable objects and toggle their active state instead of Instantiate/Destroy.
Profiler check
Look for scripting allocations per frame and GC spikes in the Profiler to confirm reduced churn.

screens.title: Asset Bundles for dynamic loading
screens.subtitle: Load, use, and unload bundles to manage large content sets

narration.text: Asset Bundles let you package assets separately and load them at runtime so you don't keep every asset resident in memory. The basic pattern is: build bundles offline, place them on disk or server, load a bundle at runtime when its content is needed, instantiate assets from the bundle, and finally unload the bundle to free memory once the assets are no longer required. The example in this chapter shows the sequence of asynchronous calls: load the bundle file, load a specific asset like a GameObject from the bundle, instantiate it, and then call Unload on the bundle when done. Note the Unload call takes a boolean parameter that controls whether assets already loaded remain in memory or not; unloading with false frees only the bundle container while keeping loaded assets. A common misconception is that loading bundles automatically frees memory when you destroy the bundle reference — you must call Unload to release the bundle data. Example workflow: load level-specific bundles at level start, instantiate needed objects, and unload bundles for previously completed levels. This keeps peak memory lower and enables modular downloadable content. How would you design a loading schedule to avoid spikes during gameplay?

keyIdea.title: Asset Bundle pattern
keyIdea.text: Load bundles on demand, instantiate assets, and call Unload(false) when you want to free bundle memory but keep already-instantiated assets.

content.html:
Architecture
Asset Bundles for dynamic loading
A simple loading, instantiate, and unload pattern keeps memory bounded.
Flow
Build bundles, download or load them from file, load assets asynchronously, instantiate, and call Unload when appropriate to free the bundle's memory.
Important detail
Unloading the bundle with false keeps assets you already loaded alive; unloading with true destroys them as well.
Misconception
Releasing the reference to an AssetBundle object is not enough — call Unload to reclaim its memory footprint.
Key Takeaway

Asset Bundles let you keep peak memory low by loading only the necessary content and unloading bundles when they are no longer needed.

Code walkthrough (visual)
// Example of loading an Asset Bundle (simplified) IEnumerator LoadAssetBundleAndObject(string bundlePath, string assetName) { // Load the bundle AssetBundleCreateRequest request = AssetBundle.LoadFromFileAsync(bundlePath); yield return request; AssetBundle bundle = request.assetBundle; if (bundle == null) { Debug.LogError("Failed to load AssetBundle!"); yield break; } // Load a specific asset from the bundle AssetBundleRequest assetRequest = bundle.LoadAssetAsync<GameObject>(assetName); yield return assetRequest; GameObject loadedObject = assetRequest.asset as GameObject; Instantiate(loadedObject); // Unload the bundle to free memory (important!) bundle.Unload(false); // 'false' means don't unload assets already loaded into memory }
The example shows asynchronous loading and a final Unload call. Use false to keep instantiated objects alive while releasing the bundle's internal memory.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: texture and audio optimization
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab: measure, change import settings, re-measure

narration.text: This lab walks you through a concrete optimization: import a high-resolution texture and a long audio clip, measure, optimize, and verify. First, create a new Unity project and import a 4096 texture and a 5-minute audio file. Place the texture on a GameObject and attach the audio to an AudioSource. Run the Profiler and capture a Memory snapshot to record baseline usage for Textures and Audio. Next, select the texture in the Project window and change Max Size to 1024 or 512 depending on its on-screen importance. Choose a compressed format appropriate for your target platform — for Android use ETC2, for iOS PVRTC, for desktop DXT — and enable or disable mip maps based on whether the texture will be seen at variable distances. Apply the changes. For audio, select Streaming as the Load Type, pick Vorbis for Compression Format, and set Quality around 70 to 80 percent; reduce sample rate if the sound can tolerate it. Run the same scene and capture a second Memory snapshot on the target device. Compare before and after to see reductions in the Textures and Audio categories. This repeatable procedure teaches you to measure before you change and to validate improvements on actual hardware.

keyIdea.title: Lab procedure
keyIdea.text: Measure baseline with the Memory profiler, change one import setting at a time, then re-measure on target hardware to confirm savings.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough
Hands-on activity: texture and audio optimization
A step-by-step lab to measure and reduce memory for textures and audio.
Step 1 — Baseline
Import a 4096 texture and 5-minute audio. Place in scene and capture Memory snapshot on device.
Step 2 — Texture
Change Max Size to 1024 or 512, pick platform format (ETC2/PVRTC/DXT), and toggle mip maps appropriately. Apply and re-run snapshot.
Step 3 — Audio
Set Load Type to Streaming, Compression to Vorbis at ~70–80% quality, and lower sample rate if acceptable. Re-run snapshot.
Compare snapshots
Look at Textures and Audio categories to quantify memory reductions. Capture screenshots for documentation.
Repeatability
Change one setting at a time to know which action produced the improvement.
Key Takeaway

The profiler proves results. Measure before and after each import change on the target device to confirm real memory savings.

screens.title: Common mistakes and verification checklist
screens.subtitle: Avoid these pitfalls and confirm success with measurable checks

narration.text: Developers commonly make a few repeatable mistakes when optimizing memory. The first is assuming disk size equals runtime memory — uncompressed runtime representations and mip maps determine R A M. Second, keeping everything loaded at startup rather than loading on demand leads to high peak memory; Asset Bundles are the remedy for modular loading. Third, leaving long music as decompressed audio leads to unnecessarily high audio memory; streaming is the better choice for long clips. Fourth, creating objects inside hot loops causes allocations and GC spikes; pooling fixes this. To verify improvements, use a short checklist: capture profiler snapshots on device before changes, change a single import setting, capture a second snapshot, and compare the Textures/Audio/Mesh categories. Also observe garbage collection frequency and per-frame scripting allocations. For final validation run a full playthrough and watch for frame-time spikes. Example assessment: after switching a long track to Streaming and reducing a texture from 4096 to 1024, you should see a measurable drop in Audio and Texture categories and a more stable frame time. End with this reflection: which of these common mistakes is most likely in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Verification checklist
keyIdea.text: Measure on device, change one setting at a time, compare profiler snapshots, and confirm that frame-time and GC behavior improved.

content.html:
Comparison
Common mistakes and verification checklist
What to avoid and how to prove your optimizations worked.
Common mistakes
  • Relying on disk size instead of runtime memory measurements.
  • Loading all assets at startup instead of on demand.
  • Leaving long audio as decompressed in memory.
  • Allocating in hot paths, causing GC spikes.
Verification checklist
  1. Capture baseline snapshot on target device.
  2. Change one import setting and re-run same scenario.
  3. Compare snapshots and inspect Textures/Audio/Mesh categories.
  4. Observe GC frequency and frame-time stability during a full playthrough.
Example confirmation
After reducing texture max size and switching audio to Streaming, both categories should show lower memory in the second snapshot and frame-time should be more stable.
Key Takeaway

Avoid these common mistakes and always verify with before/after profiler snapshots on the target hardware.

Quick reflection
Question
Which asset category is the largest in your current project, and what one change could you make to reduce it?
Pro tip
Automate baseline snapshots for builds so regressions in memory usage are caught early in CI.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Core terms and short definitions from this chapter

narration.text: These are the compact concepts you should keep in mind. Texture Compression reduces memory and uses formats like DXT, ETC, or PVRTC depending on platform. Mip Maps are precomputed smaller texture levels that improve sampling at the cost of about one-third more texture memory. Audio Load Type determines how audio is kept in memory: Decompress On Load for short effects, Compressed In Memory for medium clips, and Streaming for long music or dialogue to limit R A M usage. Each of these choices directly affects your runtime memory profile, so use the profiler to confirm the impact. Recall these terms when you inspect the Memory profiler and make import choices for your project. Key Concepts — What to Remember
Texture Compression
Use DXT, ETC, or PVRTC to reduce texture memory and match GPU formats.
Mip Maps
Smaller precomputed texture levels that improve sampling but increase memory by ~33%.
Audio Load Type
Choose Streaming for long music, Decompress On Load for short effects, or Compressed In Memory for mid-size clips.
Summary
These settings are the primary levers for reducing runtime memory. Always verify with the Memory profiler on the target hardware.

narration.text: A few final concepts complete the memory optimization picture. Asset Bundles allow you to package and load content on demand so large games don't keep everything in memory. The Memory Profiler shows breakdowns by asset category and is the authoritative source for measuring impact. Garbage Collection reclaims unused memory, but frequent GC indicates allocation churn and can cause frame hitches; reduce allocations via pooling and reuse.
